title: Share-Alike Breach in Copyleft Licences Under Indian Copyright Law: A Doctrinal Test for Distinguishing Infringement from Contractual Breach
content: Copyleft licences use copyright to keep derivative works open by conditioning permission to adapt and distribute on share-alike terms. This paper addresses a single question: when a downstream licensee in India distributes a derivative work without complying with a share-alike condition, is the conduct copyright infringement, breach of contract, or both? The Copyright Act, 1957 does not mention copyleft, and no Indian decision directly addressing it has been identified. The paper argues that the answer lies in the legal function of the term breached, not in the label “copyleft.” Section 51(a)(i) of the Act deems copyright infringed where an exclusive right is exercised in contravention of the conditions of a licence, which supports treating the breach of a term that defines the scope of the grant as infringement, while an independent promise sounds in contract. Drawing on comparative reasoning in United States decisions and on the structure of the GNU General Public License, version 3, and Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0, the paper proposes a five-step test: establish the licence, identify the exclusive right exercised, classify the term as condition or covenant, characterise the breach in light of statutory exceptions, and select proportionate remedies. The paper concludes that Indian law can accommodate copyleft without new legislation if licences separate conditions from covenants and courts classify breach by substance rather than label.
